newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: CRICKET-ARTIFICIAL LIGHT THE WAY AHEAD, SAYS BACHER.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-ARTIFICIAL LIGHT THE WAY AHEAD, SAYS BACHER.

text.p: Floodlit test cricket could soon become reality following the experimental use of lights in a first-class match in South Africa over the weekend.

Artificial lighting was used at Kingsmead on Saturday on the second day of the four-day Supersport Series match between Natal and Border when umpire Wilf Diedricks, concerned about the fading light, signalled for the five floodlights at the test ground to be switched on.
Ali Bacher, managing director of the United Cricket Board of South Africa (UCBSA), is convinced playing under lights represents the future of the game.
"We're very happy about it. We believe it is the right decision and in the best interests of first-class cricket here in South Africa," said Bacher.

"It just makes absolute sense from a cricketing point of view. If you have excellent lighting at grounds - as we do here in South Africa - then it must be used when the light isn't too good and when it curtails play for the day.

"Artificial lighting in the first-class game has got to be good for cricket, for the spectators, for the players and for the competition. Importantly, the increased playing time will mean more outright wins than previously."
The Durban experiment with artificial lighting was being keenly followed by other test-playing countries, UCBSA president Krish Mackerdhuj told Reuters.

"The other test nations are awaiting a report from us on this experiment, and in particular countries like Australia where the floodlighting is good. Brisbane has similar hours of light to Durban and their cricket officials have taken special interest in what we are doing here."
The lights at Kingsmead came on with 20 overs still to be bowled in the day but ironically the players had to come off six overs later because of poor vision.
Umpire Diedricks said: "The batsmen and the wicketkeeper weren't able to see the ball at one end because of shadows and the light reflecting off the white sightscreen."

Bacher insists such problems are surmountable. "I was reassured by Border wicketkeeper Steve Palframan there were no problems with the upright sightscreen at the one end. It was only at the other end where picking up the ball was a problem. This we can correct and I don't believe there'll be any more problems."
First-class cricket was played under lights in Australia two years ago, prompted by declining crowds at Sheffield Shield matches.
Australia pioneered the use of floodlights with the launch of Kerry Packer's rebel World Series Cricket in 1977.
